title: AppExchange evaluation, package types, licensing, risk, and installation practices
objectives: Evaluate an AppExchange listing for security review, publisher, and fit before any install.
Contrast managed versus unmanaged package types, including what remains upgradable and what becomes yours.
Explain package licensing (user licenses vs site/unlimited, Manage Package Licenses) as distinct from Salesforce user licenses.
Install with Download AppExchange Packages permission, prefer sandbox, then configure—knowing managed packages restrict some edits for future compatibility.
diagnostic_question: A VP wants a listed AppExchange app installed in production this afternoon. What package type, license, and risk questions do you ask before clicking Install, and where do you install first?
definition: AppExchange is Salesforce's marketplace for packages. A package is managed or unmanaged (Package Type on Installed Package detail). Managed packages stay upgradable by the publisher, use licenses you assign (or a site license for everyone), and lock some components so future versions still work. Unmanaged packages copy components into your org for you to own—no publisher upgrade path. Installing requires the Download AppExchange Packages permission; you can install on production or sandbox. After install, configure before users rely on it. ([View Installed Package Details](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=distribution_package_detail.htm); [Configure Installed Packages](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.distribution_configuring_packages.htm); [Install managed package example](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.einstein_data_detect_install_package.htm))
why_it_matters: Interviewers fail people who install unmanaged in production because it 'is easier,' who skip sandbox, who confuse Salesforce user licenses with package licenses, or who customize managed components that Help says you must not change if you want future versions. Security and vendor lock-in are the real risk conversation.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of a farmers market with a test kitchen. AppExchange evaluation is walking the stalls: who baked this, was it inspected, does it fit our kitchen. A managed package is a branded franchise stall—the baker still ships updates; you license seats or the whole market (site license). An unmanaged package is a basket of ingredients that become yours—no more franchise updates. Installation practice is cook in the test kitchen (sandbox) before the dining room (production). Risk is food safety plus whether you can still change the recipe.
deeper_explanation: Installed Package detail shows package type (managed or unmanaged), first installed version for managed packages, allowed and used licenses if the managed package is licensed, and actions: Uninstall, Manage Licenses, View Dependencies. Uninstall removes the package and its components. ([View Installed Package Details](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=distribution_package_detail.htm))

Manage Licenses assigns purchased licenses to users. Help states you cannot assign licenses in Lightning Experience—switch to Salesforce Classic. If you purchased a site license, or the managed package is not licensed, Salesforce assigns licenses to all users and you cannot manage them; users still need appropriate permissions. Allowed Licenses shows Unlimited for a site license. ([View Installed Package Details](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=distribution_package_detail.htm))

Download AppExchange Packages is the permission cited to install managed packages and to uninstall. Customize Application is cited to configure installed packages. After installation, components are immediately available; Help still tells you to make necessary changes before making the package available to users. All packages are customizable, but some aspects of managed packages cannot be changed to keep future versions compatible—see Components Available in Managed Packages in the packaging guide. ([Configure Installed Packages](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.distribution_configuring_packages.htm); [Data Detect install](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.einstein_data_detect_install_package.htm))

Help examples state you can install a managed package on a production or sandbox org (Field Service) and that some packages should be installed in production and sandboxes with access controls afterward (Data Detect). Prefer sandbox-first as practice even when production install is technically allowed. Third-party access prompts can appear; approving them is a risk decision, not a reflex. ([Field Service install](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.pfs_install.htm))

Unlocked packages and second-generation managed packaging are neighboring DevOps/packaging topics. Security review on AppExchange listings, OAuth scopes, and data residency: Needs verification per listing. Do not invent a 'always uninstallable without data loss' guarantee.

mental_model.analogy: Farmers market plus test kitchen: evaluation = inspect the stall, managed package = franchise stall the baker still updates, unmanaged = ingredients that become yours, licensing = seat tickets vs whole-market site pass, sandbox = test kitchen, production = dining room, locked managed components = franchise recipe you must not rewrite.
useful_mapping: AppExchange listing → stall with publisher and reviews
Managed package → franchise: upgrades and licenses
Unmanaged package → ingredients you now own; no vendor upgrade
Package license → seat on that stall, not a Salesforce Cloud license
Site license → everyone may use it if they have permissions
Configure after install → mise en place before guests
View Dependencies → what the recipe relies on
where_it_breaks: Some Salesforce-owned managed packages are not optional 'stalls' (Field Service).
Unlocked packages are neither classic managed nor unmanaged.
Uninstall can be blocked by data or dependencies.
Classic-only Manage Licenses is a UI quirk, not a farmers-market rule.

teach_back_prompt: Explain managed versus unmanaged to a CIO, then say why sandbox-first still matters when Help allows production install.

Two-minute interview: evaluation, types, licensing, risk, install.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: Evaluate the AppExchange listing first. Managed means publisher upgrades and licenses; unmanaged means you own the components with no vendor upgrade. Assign package licenses in Classic unless it is a site license. Install in sandbox, then configure. Do not edit locked managed components if you want future versions.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I refuse same-day production installs without evaluation. I ask package type, license model, dependencies, uninstall story, and third-party access. Download AppExchange Packages is the install permission. Manage Package Licenses is different from a Salesforce Cloud license. Help allows production install, but practice is test kitchen first. I cite that components go live immediately after install—so access control is urgent.

terminology.plain: Salesforce's marketplace where you find and install packages.
terminology.precise: Listings that lead to package install URLs. Evaluation includes publisher, security review, reviews, and edition fit. Not the Installed Packages Setup page itself.
terminology.example: Evaluating a LAB_ listed document-generation app before sandbox install.
terminology.non_example: A zip of metadata emailed by a contractor with no listing.

terminology.boundary: ISVforce vs unmanaged sharing: neighboring packaging.

terminology.plain: A publisher-owned, typically namespaced, upgradable package, often licensed.
terminology.precise: Package Type = Managed on Installed Package detail. First Installed Version Number is recorded. Some components are not editable so future versions remain compatible. Licenses may be named or site/Unlimited.
terminology.example: Field Service managed package installed for admins only, then licensed.
terminology.non_example: An unmanaged zip whose components you now edit freely as yours.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Unlocked package: 2GP neighbor, not this classic dichotomy.
terminology.boundary: Namespace and IP protection details: packaging guide.

terminology.plain: A bundle whose components become yours after install; the vendor does not upgrade it as a package.
terminology.precise: Package Type = Unmanaged. No first-installed-version field in the managed sense cited for managed packages. Treat as your metadata forever. Harder to unwind than a clean managed uninstall if you have customized heavily.
terminology.example: An old sample app copied into the org as unmanaged components.
terminology.non_example: A managed ISV app you expect to upgrade next quarter.
terminology.boundary: Once installed, uniqueness of API names can collide with your metadata.

terminology.plain: A seat (or site pass) for that installed managed app, not a Sales Cloud license.
terminology.precise: Allowed Licenses vs Used Licenses on the package. Site license or unlicensed managed package → all users, not manageable. Assign named licenses in Classic with Manage Package Licenses. Users still need object permissions.
terminology.example: 10 allowed licenses, 7 used, assigned in Classic.
terminology.non_example: Assigning a Salesforce Platform license and assuming the ISV app is included.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Permission set license from Salesforce (sometimes used alongside packages).
terminology.boundary: Lightning assignment UI: Help says switch to Classic.

terminology.plain: Everyone in the org may use the managed package (if they have permissions); you cannot pick seats.
terminology.precise: Allowed Licenses displays Unlimited. Salesforce assigns licenses to all users. Manage Licenses is not available for that model.
terminology.example: A site-licensed compliance app; you still restrict with profiles.
terminology.non_example: Ten named seats for power users only.
terminology.boundary: Cost model is commercial, not this Help page.

terminology.plain: The permission to install (and, per Help, uninstall) packages.
terminology.precise: Cited for install and uninstall. Distinct from Manage Package Licenses and from Customize Application (configure).
terminology.example: Admin permission set includes Download AppExchange Packages for sandbox installs.
terminology.non_example: Modify All Data alone as a substitute.
terminology.boundary: Who should hold this permission is a security design choice.

terminology.plain: The Setup record for a package already in the org.
terminology.precise: Shows type, versions, licenses, Uninstall, Manage Licenses, View Dependencies. After install, components are immediately available.
terminology.non_example: The AppExchange listing page before install.
terminology.boundary: isDeployed on some components: cited in Configure Installed Packages.

terminology.plain: The list of what the package relies on inside itself or the org.

interview_questions.question: Managed versus unmanaged packages?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Managed is publisher-upgradable and often licensed, with some locked components. Unmanaged copies components into your org; you own them and the vendor will not upgrade that package. Package Type on Installed Package detail tells you which you have.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I look at First Installed Version only on managed. I assign licenses only for licensed managed apps, in Classic if named. I will not promise an unmanaged 'upgrade next quarter.' Unlocked packages are a neighboring 2GP topic I will not fake. Uninstall removes components—View Dependencies first.
interview_questions.example: ISV doc-gen = managed. Old sample utilities = unmanaged you now maintain.

interview_questions.question: How do package licenses work?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: They are seats for that managed app, not Sales Cloud licenses. Named seats are assigned in Classic. Site license is Unlimited for everyone; you cannot pick seats; profiles still gate access.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I check Allowed vs Used. I confirm Manage Package Licenses. If Lightning hides Manage Licenses, I switch to Classic as Help says. I still add object permissions. I do not give extra Salesforce licenses to fake an ISV seat.
interview_questions.example: Ten allowed, seven used; three sellers still blocked until Classic assignment.
follow_ups: Permission set licenses vs package licenses?

interview_questions.question: VP wants production install this afternoon from a tweeted AppExchange URL.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I refuse. Evaluate publisher and security, install in sandbox, configure, then production. Help allows production technically; practice does not skip the test kitchen.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I ask package type, license model, data residency, third-party access, uninstall, and who owns it. I require Download AppExchange Packages on a controlled admin. Install for Admins Only if offered. I will not Install for All Users on a first try. I document First Installed Version after go-live.
interview_questions.example: Sandbox proof Friday; production change window next week.
follow_ups: What if it is a Salesforce-owned package like Field Service?

interview_questions.question: Admins edited a managed package's namespaced class and now upgrades fail.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: That is the compatibility trap. Help says some managed aspects cannot be changed if you want future versions. Extend with your own metadata instead.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I look up Components Available in Managed Packages. I restore vendor components if possible. I put customizations in local Lightning pages, extra fields on allowed objects, or an extension package. I treat this as a risk in evaluation: how much must we customize?
interview_questions.example: Cloned a managed LWC into local namespace instead of editing the locked one.
tradeoffs: Fork vs pay the ISV for a feature

interview_questions.question: Package installed; users still cannot open it.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Check named licenses, site-versus-permission gap, and whether it was Install for Admins Only. Install success is not user access.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I open Installed Package detail. If Used Licenses is zero on a named model, assign in Classic. If site license, I fix profiles. I look at permission set licenses the package added. I do not reinstall first.
interview_questions.example: Install for Admins Only; sellers lack the permission set and package license.

interview_questions.question: Uninstall button errors.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: View Dependencies, check data in package objects, and confirm Download AppExchange Packages. Uninstall removes all components—it can be blocked.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I export or re-parent data. I remove my extra metadata that references package components. I do not delete the org. I warn that unmanaged leftovers after a partial cleanup are worse than a blocked managed uninstall.
interview_questions.example: Custom Flow references a managed object; uninstall blocked until the Flow is retired.
follow_ups: Can we hide instead of uninstall?

interview_questions.question: When would you build in-house instead of AppExchange?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: When the listing fails evaluation, when unmanaged would become unowned debt, when licenses cost more than a small Flow, or when data cannot leave the org via third-party access.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I still prefer a reviewed managed app over a random Apex blob if the ISV is a better long-term owner. I compare declarative build (AUTO-001) versus package. I include uninstall and upgrade in the TCO. I will not install a package to avoid writing a validation rule.
interview_questions.example: A three-step approval is Flow, not an ISV. A global e-sign product is AppExchange.

interview_questions.question: Teach this with the farmers-market analogy and where it breaks.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Evaluation is inspecting the stall, managed is a franchise the baker still updates, unmanaged is ingredients you own, licenses are seat tickets or a whole-market pass, sandbox is the test kitchen.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: It breaks for Salesforce-owned packages, unlocked packages, blocked uninstalls, and Classic-only Manage Licenses. I then quote Help: Package Type, site license Unlimited, Download AppExchange Packages, immediate component availability, managed compatibility locks, production-or-sandbox install with sandbox-first practice. I never skip risk: third-party access and uninstall blast radius.
interview_questions.example: Whiteboard: listing → type → licenses → sandbox → configure → production.
follow_ups: Where do Files in a package live? (APP-006)
